module_info.title: General Veterinary Pathology AI Tutor
module_info.subtitle: Module: Etiology and Classification of Disease (BVSc & AH)

session_1.title: Session 1 of 7 — What is Etiology?
session_1.salutation: Welcome, {student_name}! Department of Veterinary Pathology, CVAS, Pookode welcomes you to Session 1.
session_1.scenario: At CVAS Pookode, two calves are housed under identical management conditions on the same farm. After a sudden weather change, Calf B develops a severe cough and high fever, while Calf A remains healthy and active.
session_1.question: Why do you think Calf B became sick while Calf A stayed healthy?
options: A) Calf B just had bad luck and got tired.
B) Something specific interacted with or attacked Calf B that didn't affect Calf A.
C) Calves naturally take turns getting sick on farms.
session_1.feedback_correct: Correct! Disease occurs because a specific cause acts upon an animal.
session_1.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Think about whether a specific external or internal agent entered or acted upon Calf B.

term_card.meaning: The study of the cause or origin of disease.
term_card.example: Determining whether a cow's respiratory signs are caused by a virus, bacteria, or cold stress.

session_1.recap: Etiology asks the central question: WHY did this animal become sick?

session_2.title: Session 2 of 7 — Predisposing Causes
session_2.scenario: A herd of mixed-breed cattle is exposed to intense sunlight. White-faced Hereford cattle develop skin lesions on their unpigmented eyelids (Cancer Eye), while fully pigmented Angus cattle in the same field show no lesions.
session_2.question: What type of factor made the Hereford cattle more susceptible to skin damage?
options: B) Predisposing cause (Lack of skin pigmentation)
session_2.feedback_correct: Spot on! Lack of skin pigmentation is an intrinsic predisposing factor that increases vulnerability to UV radiation.
session_2.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Re-read the scenario—the sunlight was present for all, but skin color made one group more vulnerable.

term_card.meaning: A factor intrinsic or extrinsic to the animal that increases its susceptibility to disease without directly causing it.
term_card.example: Age, species, breed, sex, or lack of protective skin pigmentation.

session_2.recap: Predisposing causes do not directly initiate disease; they make the host more vulnerable.

session_3.title: Session 3 of 7 — Physical Causes
session_3.scenario: A dog is brought to the veterinary emergency clinic with severe soft tissue trauma and multiple bone fractures following a motor vehicle accident.
session_3.question: Which etiological category directly initiated this structural tissue damage?
options: A) Physical Cause (Mechanical Kinetic Energy / Trauma)
session_3.feedback_correct: Correct! Mechanical kinetic energy (trauma) directly caused the structural and tissue damage.
session_3.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Consider whether external kinetic force, chemicals, or living organisms caused the physical injury.

term_card.meaning: Environmental energy or forces acting on tissues (Mechanical Trauma, Extreme Heat, Cold, or Radiation).
term_card.example: Frostbite from extreme cold, burns from thermal heat, or fractures from trauma.

session_3.recap: Physical causes involve external physical forces or energy damaging body structures.

session_4.title: Session 4 of 7 — Chemical Causes and Toxins
session_4.salutation: Moving along nicely, {student_name}! Welcome to Session 4.
session_4.scenario: A farm dog accidentally ingests an open container of organophosphate pesticide stored in a barn and shows severe muscular twitching, profuse salivation, and collapse within 30 minutes.
session_4.question: How should this primary cause of illness be classified?
session_4.feedback_correct: Correct! Pesticides are toxic chemical agents that disrupt cellular and neuromuscular function.
session_4.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Think about whether the pesticide acts through living infection or chemical toxicity.

term_card.meaning: Exogenous or endogenous chemical substances that alter cell function or cause molecular cell injury.
term_card.example: Organophosphate toxicity, heavy metal poisoning, or phytotoxin ingestion.

session_4.recap: Chemicals and toxins produce disease through chemical cell injury rather than physical force.

session_5.title: Session 5 of 7 — Biological / Viable Causes
session_5.scenario: A flock of grazing sheep exhibits severe pale mucous membranes (anemia) and submandibular edema ('bottle jaw') due to a heavy Haemonchus contortus parasite infestation in the abomasum.
session_5.question: What broad etiological category does Haemonchus contortus belong to?
session_5.feedback_correct: Correct! Helminths and parasites are living (viable) biological agents that invade and parasitize host tissues.
session_5.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Is Haemonchus contortus a living biological organism or an inorganic force?

term_card.meaning: Living infectious micro- or macro-organisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi, mycoplasma, rickettsia, and parasites.
term_card.example: Foot-and-Mouth Disease virus in cattle, Anthrax bacteria in sheep, or Haemonchus worms.

session_5.recap: Biological causes are living, replicating agents that infect or parasitize animal tissues.

session_6.title: Session 6 of 7 — Nutritional & Immunological Causes
session_6.salutation: Almost at the finish line, {student_name}! Welcome to Session 6.
session_6.scenario: A high-yielding dairy cow collapses shortly after calving and cannot stand up. Blood tests reveal acute serum calcium depletion (Milk Fever / Parturient Paresis).
session_6.question: What etiological category best describes Milk Fever?
session_6.feedback_correct: Exactly right! Acute metabolic deficiency of calcium around calving causes milk fever.
session_6.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Consider whether acute lack of an essential mineral relates to metabolic/nutritional balance.

term_card.meaning: Disease resulting from acute or chronic deficiency, excess, or metabolic imbalance of essential nutrients.
term_card.example: Vitamin B1 deficiency causing cerebrocortical necrosis in sheep, or Hypocalcemia in dairy cows.

session_6.recap: Nutritional and metabolic causes stem from imbalances in essential elements required for systemic function.

session_7.title: Session 7 of 7 — Complete Classification & Consolidation
session_7.salutation: Final session, {student_name}! Let's consolidate everything you have learned.
session_7.scenario: A dog develops severe facial swelling, respiratory distress, and systemic collapse (anaphylaxis) within 5 minutes of receiving a wasp sting.
session_7.question: Which etiological category primarily drives this acute allergic reaction?
session_7.feedback_correct: Excellent! Anaphylaxis is an extreme, rapid immunological hypersensitivity reaction.
session_7.feedback_incorrect: Good attempt! Re-read the scenario—the body's own immune system overreacted violently to the venom allergen.

term_card.meaning: Systematic organization of all disease causes into Predisposing and Definitive categories.
term_card.example: Review the full summary matrix generated on your final completion screen.

session_7.recap: You have successfully mastered all 7 micro-sessions in Veterinary Etiology!

Mechanical, thermal, cold, or radiation forces
rows.example: Traumatic bone fractures from vehicle accidents
